name: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures
aliases: Malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy

clinicalPearls: A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy of early infancy, usually beginning in the first months of life (before six months of age) in an infant who may initially have appeared well.

The defining feature is migrating focal seizures — ictal discharges arise independently from multiple shifting cortical regions, and a single seizure can migrate from one area or hemisphere to another.
Seizures become very frequent, often near-continuous, and are typically highly drug-resistant.
Gain-of-function variants in KCNT1 (a sodium-activated potassium channel) are the most common cause; other genes include SCN2A, SCN1A, SCN8A, SLC12A5 and TBC1D24.
Developmental arrest or regression with acquired microcephaly and axial hypotonia is characteristic as seizures intensify.
EEG shows multifocal abnormalities with the characteristic ictal pattern of discharges migrating between independent foci; early brain imaging is often normal.
Response to standard antiseizure medicines is generally poor; quinidine has been trialled as a targeted therapy in KCNT1-related disease with variable and unpredictable benefit.
Treatable structural, metabolic and, where relevant, infective mimics must be excluded before the diagnosis is accepted.
reference.pathophysiology: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures is most often a channelopathy. Gain-of-function variants in KCNT1 augment the sodium-activated potassium current, altering neuronal firing properties and network excitability in a way that paradoxically favours hyperexcitability and the emergence of multiple, spatially independent seizure foci that migrate across the cortex. Other causative genes affect voltage-gated sodium channels (SCN1A, SCN2A and SCN8A), the neuronal potassium-chloride cotransporter (SLC12A5, encoding KCC2) that sets the chloride gradient underpinning inhibitory GABAergic signalling, and synaptic and vesicular proteins. Relentless multifocal epileptic activity during a critical period of brain maturation drives the encephalopathy — developmental slowing or regression and impaired head growth — so that both the underlying cause and the ongoing seizures contribute to the disability, in keeping with the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy designation.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (early-infantile encephalopathy and Dravet syndrome)
Glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) deficiency and other treatable metabolic epilepsies
Structural cortical malformations such as hemimegalencephaly and focal cortical dysplasia
Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with neonatal or infantile seizures
Central nervous system infection or hypoxic-ischaemic injury as acquired causes
Self-limited familial or non-familial infantile epilepsy, which has a very different and favourable course
additionalInvestigations: Prolonged video-EEG to capture the migrating ictal pattern
Brain MRI, often normal early, to exclude structural causes and provide a baseline
Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome or genome sequencing (KCNT1 and related genes)
Metabolic work-up including investigations for treatable causes such as vitamin-responsive and glucose-transporter-related epilepsies
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis with paired plasma glucose, lactate and neurotransmitter studies, and exclusion of infection
A supervised trial of pyridoxine or pyridoxal phosphate and consideration of the ketogenic diet where a treatable cause is plausible
redFlags: Near-continuous or rapidly escalating seizures, or status epilepticus
Developmental regression and deceleration of head growth
Apnoea, autonomic instability or feeding failure during seizure clusters
Failure to consider and test for treatable metabolic causes before accepting the diagnosis
Features suggesting an alternative acute cause such as infection or metabolic decompensation requiring urgent treatment
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally poor, with most children having drug-resistant seizures, severe global developmental impairment and an increased risk of early mortality; only a minority achieve meaningful seizure control. Outcome may be modified where a treatable underlying cause is identified early or, in selected KCNT1 cases, where targeted therapy provides benefit.
pitfalls: Missing a treatable metabolic epilepsy, such as a vitamin-responsive or glucose-transporter disorder, by not testing before labelling the disorder as EIMFS.
Assuming quinidine will help all KCNT1 cases — the response is inconsistent and it carries cardiac (QT prolongation) risk requiring monitoring.
Under-recognising the migrating ictal pattern because the EEG recording was not sufficiently prolonged.
Interpreting an initially normal MRI as reassurance and delaying genetic and metabolic work-up.
Confusing it with self-limited (benign) infantile epilepsy, which has a completely different and favourable outlook.
management: Trial antiseizure medications recognising frequent drug resistance, and consider quinidine as a targeted option in KCNT1 gain-of-function disease, while avoiding sodium-channel blockers that may worsen some genotypes
Institute the ketogenic diet as an adjunctive treatment for refractory seizures
Trial pyridoxine or pyridoxal phosphate and treat any identified treatable cause, such as the ketogenic diet for glucose-transporter deficiency
Provide supportive care with developmental therapies, feeding and nutritional support and respiratory care for this encephalopathy
Equip families with rescue benzodiazepines and a status epilepticus plan for prolonged or clustering seizures
Arrange epilepsy gene testing and genetic counselling for KCNT1 and related genes
Offer palliative care and psychosocial family support given the guarded prognosis, coordinated by paediatric neurology
